title: Best Practices & Clean Code
description: Habits that keep code readable, testable and safe to change — and how teams work together.
resumo: Organize by feature; controllers return DTOs; no catch-all Utils class.
SRP, DRY (same knowledge, not same text), KISS, YAGNI.
Names reveal intent and side effects; comments explain why, not what.
Name your SQL columns, parameterize, paginate, version the schema.
Test the error contract (400, 404, 409), not only the happy path.
One change per commit, small PRs, Conventional Commits.
Log once, with context and placeholders; never secrets or personal data.
Measure before optimizing; change one thing at a time.
Access control checks ownership, not only login (OWASP Top 10).

subsections.subtitle: Code Organization
subsections.description: A structure where everyone knows where things go.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a new developer opens the project and finds `Util2`, 800-line services and no way to tell where a new class should go.

**Concept:** a consistent structure — packages by feature, with controller, service and repository inside — plus names that reveal intent and small classes with one responsibility. Javadoc is for public APIs and non-obvious decisions, not for repeating what the code says.

**How it works:** when you add something, put it next to the feature it belongs to. Controllers return DTOs, never entities.
examples.code:
com.shop
 ├── orders
 │    ├── OrderController
 │    ├── OrderService
 │    ├── OrderRepository
 │    └── dto/ (CreateOrderRequest, OrderResponse)
 └── catalog
      └── ...

/**
 * Lists the products of a category.
 * @param category the category slug, e.g. "books"
 * @return the products, as DTOs (not entities)
 */
@GetMapping("/products")
public List<ProductResponse> listByCategory(@RequestParam String category) {
    return service.listByCategory(category);
}
examples.interview_question: How do you organize the code of a backend project?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A catch-all `Utils` class. Unrelated static methods pile up in it, everything depends on it, and nobody knows what is inside. Put each helper next to the code that uses it, or in a small class with a clear name.

subsections.subtitle: Design Principles: SRP, DRY, KISS and YAGNI
subsections.description: Four short rules that keep code easy to change.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the same rule is duplicated in five places and one of them is forgotten in the next change; or an elaborate abstraction was built for a case that never came.

**Concept:** SRP (Single Responsibility): a class has one reason to change. DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself): each piece of knowledge has one representation in the code. KISS (Keep It Simple): the simplest solution that works. YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It): do not build features or extension points before they are needed.

**How it works:** they balance each other: DRY removes duplication, while KISS and YAGNI stop you from building abstractions too early.
examples.interview_question: What are SRP, DRY, KISS and YAGNI, and how do you apply them?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Applying DRY to code that only looks alike. Two rules that happen to have the same formula today are merged, and when one of them changes, the other breaks. DRY is about the same knowledge, not the same text.

subsections.subtitle: Databases
subsections.description: Everyday practices for the data layer.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** most production performance problems and data bugs start in the database layer: slow queries, missing transactions, schema differences between environments.

**Concept:** select only the columns you need; index the columns you filter and join on; always use parameterized queries; wrap related writes in one transaction; version the schema with migrations (Flyway); paginate lists. Each item has its own lesson in the Databases topic.

**How it works:** check new queries with `EXPLAIN` and the SQL log before they reach production.
examples.interview_question: Which practices do you follow to write efficient and safe SQL?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: `SELECT *` in application code. It fetches columns nobody uses — sometimes large ones — prevents index-only scans, and changes silently when a column is added. Name the columns.

subsections.subtitle: APIs and Testing
subsections.description: APIs that are predictable, and tests that keep them that way.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** an API without tests breaks its clients silently: a renamed field, a status code that changed, a validation that disappeared.

**Concept:** design clear resource URLs, return the right status codes, validate input with `@Valid`, return errors as Problem Details, and test at every level: unit tests for rules, slices for controllers, a few end-to-end tests for critical flows.

**How it works:** RestAssured (or Karate) calls the running application over HTTP, the way a client does.
examples.interview_question: How do you make sure a REST API stays reliable?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Testing only the happy path. The 400, 404 and 409 responses are part of the contract, and they are the ones that break without anyone noticing.

subsections.subtitle: Git and Collaboration
subsections.description: A history and a workflow the team can rely on.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** an unreadable history, huge pull requests and constant conflicts slow the whole team down.

**Concept:** small commits with clear messages (Conventional Commits), short branches named after the task, pull requests reviewed by a teammate, and a `.gitignore` from day one. Each item has its own lesson in the Version Control topic.

**How it works:** integrate with main often, and keep each pull request about one thing.
examples.code:
git switch -c feature/new-api
git commit -m "feat(products): add GET /products endpoint"
git push -u origin feature/new-api
# open a pull request, get a review, merge
examples.interview_question: How do you organize commits in a team project?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Unrelated changes in one commit. It cannot be reverted without undoing the other changes, and the message cannot describe it.
examples.code:
# WRONG
git commit -m "feat: login + fix typo + bump dependencies"

# RIGHT: one change per commit
git commit -m "feat(auth): add login endpoint"
git commit -m "fix(docs): correct README typo"
git commit -m "chore(deps): upgrade spring boot to 3.3.5"

subsections.subtitle: Agile Teams and Scrum
subsections.description: How work is organized in sprints.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the team plans everything upfront, delivers months later, and finds out the plan was wrong.

**Concept:** agile methods deliver software in short cycles and use feedback from each delivery instead of planning everything at the start. In Scrum, work happens in sprints of one to four weeks. Roles: the Product Owner orders the backlog; the Scrum Master removes impediments and looks after the process; the Developers build. Events: Sprint Planning (what goes into the sprint), the Daily (15 minutes for the team to inspect progress toward the sprint goal), Sprint Review (show what was delivered) and the Retrospective (how to improve the process). Kanban is the alternative without sprints: continuous flow with a limit on work in progress.

**How it works:** a task is done only when it meets the team's Definition of Done — usually tests, approved code review and a green pipeline. The "yesterday, today, blockers" format for the Daily is common, but the Scrum Guide no longer requires it (since 2020).
examples.code:
Example Daily:
Yesterday: finished the jackson-databind upgrade and opened the PR.
Today: address the review comments and start the Karate tests for the orders endpoint.
Blocker: I need access to the QA environment.

Definition of Done (example):
[ ] Code reviewed and approved
[ ] Unit and API tests passing
[ ] No new high or critical CVE in the scan
[ ] Pipeline green
[ ] The story's acceptance criteria met
examples.interview_question: What are the Scrum events, and what is each one for?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Turning the Daily into a status report to a manager. Everyone talks to one person, nobody coordinates, and blockers wait for the meeting. The Daily is for the developers to plan the next 24 hours together; raise a blocker as soon as it appears.

subsections.subtitle: Performance and DevOps
subsections.description: Measure first, then optimize — and automate delivery.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** optimizing by guessing: weeks spent tuning code that was never the bottleneck.

**Concept:** measure before changing anything (metrics, profiling, `EXPLAIN`), then fix the biggest bottleneck. Common wins: caching read-heavy data, moving non-urgent work out of the request (`@Async` or a queue), small Docker images, and an automated CI/CD pipeline with monitoring (Prometheus) to see the effect.

**How it works:** change one thing at a time and measure again; otherwise you never know what helped.
examples.code:
name: CI
on: [push]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { distribution: temurin, java-version: '21', cache: maven }
      - run: ./mvnw -B verify
examples.interview_question: Which practices would you use to make deployments and the application faster?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Optimizing without measuring. A cache is added for a slow endpoint; the real problem was a missing index, and now there is a cache to keep consistent as well.
examples.code:
WRONG: endpoint slow -> add a Redis cache -> still slow on cache misses, plus stale data

RIGHT: endpoint slow -> look at metrics and the SQL log -> EXPLAIN shows a Seq Scan
       -> add the index -> measure again

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** `int d; List<int[]> lst = get(1);` — reading the code means guessing what each name means.

**Concept:** names should reveal intent: what it is, why it exists, how it is used. Prefer domain terms (`calculateShipping`, `pendingOrders`) to abbreviations (`calc`, `lst`, `tmp`). Methods are verbs, classes are nouns, booleans read like questions (`isActive`, `hasStock`). When a comment explains *what* the code does, a better name or an extracted method usually removes the need; comments are for the *why*.

**How it works:** rename freely — the IDE does it safely — whenever a name stops matching what the code does.
examples.interview_question: How do good names reduce the need for comments?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A name that hides a side effect. `checkUser` sounds like a read, but it also writes to the database. Name it for everything it does, or split it.

subsections.subtitle: Logging and Error Handling
subsections.description: Failing in a visible, diagnosable way.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a production error with no log, or the same error logged four times with no context — either way, nobody can tell what happened.

**Concept:** never swallow exceptions (empty `catch`). Use the right levels: ERROR for failures that need action, WARN for abnormal but recoverable situations, INFO for business events, DEBUG for diagnosis. Include context (order and user ids) with SLF4J placeholders, and never log passwords, tokens or personal data.

**How it works:** pass the exception as the last argument, so the stack trace is logged.
examples.interview_question: Which common mistakes do you avoid when handling exceptions and writing logs?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Logging and rethrowing in every layer. The same error appears in the log once per layer, and it looks like four problems. Log it once, where it is handled.

subsections.subtitle: Code Review
subsections.description: Reviews that improve the code and the team.

examples.title: Reviewing a Pull Request
examples.explanation:
Start with the goal: does the PR solve the problem it describes? Then correctness and edge cases, tests covering the behavior, readability and names, security (input validation, secrets) and performance impact. Small PRs get reviewed better and faster.

Keep comments objective and about the code, not the person, and say which ones are blocking and which are suggestions.
examples.code:
Review checklist:
[ ] The description explains what changes and why
[ ] There are tests for the new behavior and for the error cases
[ ] No secret, password or sensitive data in the code or the logs
[ ] External input is validated
[ ] New queries do not cause N+1 or load too much data
[ ] CI is green
examples.interview_question: What do you look for when reviewing a pull request?

examples.title: Receiving a Review
examples.explanation:
A good pull request makes the review easy: one subject per PR, and a description with what changes, why, and how it was tested, plus a link to the task or the CVE. Comments are about the code, not about you: answer every one, fix what is requested or explain with arguments why you would keep it, and resolve a thread only after handling it.

When a discussion gets long, a quick call settles it better than ten comments. For an intern, reviewing teammates' PRs is also a great way to learn the codebase.
examples.code:
PR description template:

## What changes
Upgrades jackson-databind from 2.17.1 to 2.17.2.

## Why
Fixes CVE-XXXX-YYYY (CVSS 7.5), reported by Dependency-Check.

## How it was tested
- mvn verify (unit and integration)
- Karate tests for the customers API in the QA environment

## Task
JIRA-123
examples.interview_question: How do you react when your pull request gets many comments?

subsections.subtitle: Security Basics (OWASP)
subsections.description: The most common risks in web applications.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** most breaches exploit a short list of well-known mistakes, not exotic attacks.

**Concept:** the OWASP Top 10 lists the most critical risks in web applications. Among them: broken access control (check that the user may access *that* resource, not only that they are logged in), injection (use parameterized queries), cryptographic failures (HTTPS, and passwords hashed with BCrypt) and vulnerable components (keep dependencies updated and scanned in CI). Secrets go in environment variables or vaults, never in the repository.

**How it works:** check ownership in the query itself, so another user's data never even loads. Returning 404 for someone else's resource also avoids revealing that it exists.
examples.interview_question: Name OWASP Top 10 risks and how to mitigate them in a Java API.

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Checking only that the user is logged in. Any authenticated user reads any order just by changing the id in the URL (an IDOR, insecure direct object reference).
